top_line: Cost-of-living protests turned into France's worst rioting in years, pushing up French borrowing costs and spreading to Italy, Belgium, Albania and Portugal. Meanwhile the Houthis carried out the deadliest strike of Yemen's renewed war, and Zelensky said US policy looks like pushing Ukraine to surrender.

stories.headline: France imposes local curfews after a weekend of riots and looting, as its bonds sell off and unrest spreads across Europe
stories.what_happened: More than half a million people joined cost-of-living protests across France at the weekend, and in cities including Paris, Marseille and Limoges they turned into rioting, looting and clashes with outnumbered police, with about 2,400 arrests. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police 'lost control' and offered his resignation, which President Macron refused. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered localised partial curfews and a large operation to identify suspects. He blamed the 'ultra-left' for exploiting the protests and said it was 'a miracle' that no one was killed. French bonds and shares sold off and the gap with German borrowing costs widened. Looting and clashes were also reported in Milan, Brussels, Liège and Tirana.
stories.why_it_matters: The unrest comes about six months before France's presidential election. The National Rally, already ahead in the polls, is presenting itself as the party of order, and Macron faces criticism from all sides. The bond sell-off shows how quickly social instability affects a heavily indebted state's finances. Oxford Economics warns that a severe bond shock could push France and Italy into recession in 2027, though that is not its central forecast.

whats_new.before: French school protests had already turned violent earlier this month, with nearly 2,000 arrests, and the government was under fiscal pressure.
whats_new.now: The protests have become nationwide cost-of-living unrest with mass looting, a minister's offered resignation, curfews and a market reaction, and similar protests are spreading to other European countries.

stories.headline: Houthi missiles kill at least 53 at a Yemeni government training camp, as Saudi Arabia postpones its flagship investment forum
stories.what_happened: A Houthi ballistic missile attack on a government security forces training camp in Shabwa province killed at least 53 people and injured about 200, according to local authorities. The Guardian calls it the largest single loss of life since Yemen's civil war reignited. Saudi Arabia postponed its Future Investment Initiative, due next week in Riyadh, to next year after Houthi attacks; Semafor reports that Wall Street executives had raised safety concerns. Egypt pledged 'all necessary and possible forms of support' to Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan's army said it is providing whatever support is needed.
stories.why_it_matters: The war is now hitting Saudi Arabia's economic plans and drawing in regional allies, which raises the risk of a wider conflict on the Red Sea and Gulf routes. Postponing the forum known as 'Davos in the desert' is a visible cost to Riyadh's effort to present itself as a safe place to invest.

whats_new.before: The Houthis had struck Riyadh's airport, killing 12, and Saudi Arabia had hit Houthi oil depots near Sanaa.
whats_new.now: The deadliest single attack of the renewed war has hit government forces, the investment forum has been postponed, and Egypt and Pakistan have publicly committed support.

stories.headline: Zelensky says US policy looks like pushing Ukraine to surrender, as Kyiv gets warning of only one of two missile attacks
stories.what_happened: Zelensky said he did not want to believe Washington wanted the war to end at Ukraine's expense, 'but that's how it looks'. Ukraine's air force said Western allies warned of only one of two overnight attacks; Zelensky said Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv region and more than 200 drones across the country. Secretary of State Rubio said there is no pause in US intelligence sharing. Trump blocked a number of Russia sanctions two days before they were due to take effect, saying this keeps peace negotiations going. Zelensky also said he believes the US government is behind the Ukrainian military's loss of normal access to the Starshield satellite service. Lithuanian officials say a fire at a Starlink centre was sabotage.
stories.why_it_matters: Disputes over intelligence, sanctions and satellite access go to the core of Ukraine's ability to defend itself, and they leave Europe more exposed. The FT reports that European leaders are preparing to talk to Putin directly. Drone strikes between the two sides continue; Russia's VK social network was disrupted after a drone strike on a data centre.

whats_new.before: Europe had pushed back against Trump's Russian diesel deal, and Zelensky had said Kyiv got no warning of a ballistic strike.
whats_new.now: Zelensky openly says US policy looks like pressure to surrender, more sanctions have been blocked, and a dispute over satellite access has emerged.

stories.headline: World Food Programme cuts aid to about half a million Gazans as funding runs short and ceasefire progress stalls
stories.what_happened: The UN World Food Programme said funding shortages will force it to cut assistance in Gaza by roughly a third, reducing the number of people it helps from 1.6 million to 1.1 million as winter approaches. Families who keep support will get smaller rations and less cash. The Guardian reports that two-thirds of the population face crisis levels of food insecurity and 200,000 people are in danger of famine. The WFP head said 1.4 million people face acute shortages despite the US-brokered ceasefire, and Gazans also report continuing restrictions on shipments.
stories.why_it_matters: This shows that a ceasefire does not end a hunger crisis when aid money and access are both limited. The cut comes as wider aid budgets shrink, and it adds pressure on donors and on talks over the next stage of the ceasefire.

whats_new.before: The ceasefire had allowed more food into Gaza, but needs remained very high.
whats_new.now: The main UN food agency is reducing its caseload by about a third because of funding gaps.

stories.headline: Iran hits at least 15 container ships in Hormuz in ten days, as Qatar warns the energy disruption has not yet peaked
stories.what_happened: Iran has attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz in the past ten days, some with drones, according to the Guardian, and people have been searching for spilt cargo. Qatar warned that the energy disruption is at a 'peak', with more difficulties expected in the coming days and months; it is preparing a new regional defence partnership while keeping channels open with Tehran. Pakistan, which is mediating between Iran and the US, suspended border trade with Iran, and Russia's foreign minister Lavrov visited Tehran for the first time since the war began.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on container shipping, not only tankers, spread the war's costs into global trade and supply chains. A warning from Qatar, a major gas exporter, suggests energy prices could stay under pressure into winter.

whats_new.before: Iran had hit 24 ships in Hormuz in two weeks, the worst spate of attacks of the war.
whats_new.now: Container ships are now a frequent target, and Qatar says worse disruption may still be ahead.

stories.headline: Kenya confirms an eighth Ebola case as the DR Congo outbreak reaches a new province
stories.what_happened: Kenya has confirmed an eighth case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, its first-ever cluster of the disease. The outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the second-largest in history, has killed more than 4,300 people and is still spreading to new areas. The Guardian reports opposition in Kenya to a US-led quarantine centre, after sweeping US funding cuts and the US withdrawal from the WHO.
stories.why_it_matters: Transmission in Kenya, a regional travel hub, raises the risk of further spread. This is happening while international health support is being cut, which could weaken the response.

whats_new.before: Kenya had recorded its first-ever Ebola death and was tracing the patient's contacts.

stories.headline: China's growth beats forecasts at 4.5% on AI-driven exports, as Beijing adds export controls and limits foreign biotech deals
stories.what_happened: China's GDP grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter, up from 4.3% and faster than expected. Exports of electronics and other high-tech goods drove the growth, while consumer spending stayed weak. That keeps China on track for its 4.5–5% target for 2026. On the same day, Beijing introduced export controls on tunnel-boring machines, which India wants, citing national security. STAT reports China is also proposing limits on foreign purchases of critical biopharma technology.
stories.why_it_matters: China's growth depends more and more on selling high-tech goods abroad, which makes it more exposed to trade tensions and to any downturn in AI spending. The new controls show Beijing using export rules, not only facing them, to protect industries it sees as strategic.

whats_new.before: China's growth had slowed to 4.3% in the second quarter.
whats_new.now: Growth picked up on exports, and Beijing extended controls to construction machinery and biotech deals.

stories.headline: UN nature summit opens in Armenia with none of the 2022 biodiversity targets met, as the EU awards €3.4bn to net-zero projects
stories.what_happened: COP17, the UN Biodiversity Conference, has opened in Yerevan to push governments to meet the 23 targets agreed at COP15 in 2022. A Guardian analysis finds that not one of them has yet been met. The European Commission selected 77 net-zero technology projects for €3.4bn from its Innovation Fund and granted more than €390m to 135 LIFE climate and environment projects. Separately, the FT reports that the EU's new Arctic strategy drops its 2021 pledge to work toward a global ban on new hydrocarbon development in the region, and Longyearbyen in Svalbard has told residents not to drink tap water because thawing ground is releasing heavy metals.
stories.why_it_matters: The summit will show whether the global nature deal still has momentum. EU funding is a concrete commitment, but it is offset by a softer position on Arctic drilling as energy security dominates policy.

whats_new.before: The 2022 COP15 deal set 23 targets.

stories.headline: Kenyan court convicts cult leader Paul Mackenzie of murdering 190 children and one adult
stories.what_happened: A Kenyan court found the self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of 190 children and one adult. Prosecutors say his sect ordered followers to starve themselves and their children. Hundreds of bodies had been exhumed from a remote forest. Sentencing is still to come.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the worst cult-related disasters in recent history, and the verdict is the first judgement in the case. It could renew debate in Kenya over oversight of religious groups.

stories.headline: Portugal's rent law wobbles as Chega threatens to abandon its deal with the PSD, amid housing camps and scrutiny of MPs' property
stories.what_happened: With housing protests in Lisbon and Porto, Chega said it may vote against the Government's rent law at the detailed (specialty) stage, after abstaining to let it pass the first vote. Chega also proposed an 'emergency legislative package' with higher IRS deductions and said it would accept a budget deficit to pay for it. PS leader José Luís Carneiro proposed exempting from capital-gains tax sales of existing homes up to €300,000 for one's own home, and Bloco asked the Prime Minister to withdraw the proposal. ECO reports that the 220 Government members and PSD, Chega, IL and CDS-PP MPs together own 1,039 properties worth about €55.6m; nothing in the law prevents them voting on the changes. Protesters have camped in central Lisbon, and reports say police have asked for the tents to be removed.
stories.why_it_matters: If Chega withdraws, the Government's plan to liberalise renting could fail or change substantially, which affects landlords, tenants and investors already adjusting to the new rules. The opposition's tax proposals indicate where housing tax policy may go.

whats_new.before: Parliament approved the rent law in a first vote after a PSD–Chega deal, and protesters had set up camp in Porto.
whats_new.now: Chega is threatening to break the deal, rival tax proposals have appeared, and the protest camps have reached Lisbon.

stories.headline: EU Council recommends that member states act to prevent evictions and help with rent

stories.why_it_matters: A Council recommendation is not binding, but it sets a shared policy direction alongside the EU's Affordable Housing plan and Housing Act. It may influence how governments such as Portugal's and Spain's frame tenant protections.

stories.headline: Portuguese market signals: rental confidence rises as sales confidence falls, and the Government advances a Construction Code
stories.what_happened: Idealista reports that confidence in Portugal's property market is rising for renting and falling for home sales. Portuguese property investment funds managed €21.395bn in September, up 0.1% from August, according to Jornal Económico. The Government is moving ahead with a Construction Code, and new coefficients for property capital-gains calculations have been published. Separately, vida imobiliaria reports that defence spending is driving investment in industrial and logistics property in Europe.

stories.headline: Anthropic commits 5% of its shares to a public-benefit fund before its IPO, and Musk pledges a SpaceX share to every US child
stories.what_happened: Anthropic said it will commit at least 5% of its shares to a 'public benefit fund' ahead of its expected stock market listing; the Guardian values the stake at about $48bn. Anthropic says the fund could make 'large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations', but has given few details. It also gave an outside AI watchdog 'employee-like' access, and the watchdog can publish its findings without Anthropic's approval. Hours later, Elon Musk said he would give one SpaceX share to every child in the US next year, worth about $10.7bn at Friday's close, without saying who would qualify or how it would work.
stories.why_it_matters: Analysis: AI companies are competing for public legitimacy as much as for customers, at a time when the FT describes a growing public backlash over safety and economic concerns. Reporting suggests Democrats, who polls say could win at least one chamber of Congress, plan to scrutinise the AI industry more aggressively. How the fund and the watchdog arrangement actually work will show whether this is real accountability or mainly positioning before the IPO.

whats_new.before: Anthropic had taken risky tests offline and warned that AI might soon copy itself between devices.
whats_new.now: It has committed equity to the public and given an outside watchdog independent access, and Musk has made a rival share pledge.

stories.headline: Microsoft pulls out of the UK's largest AI data centre over power supply, as Amazon funds 12 small nuclear reactors in Indiana
stories.what_happened: Microsoft has abandoned its agreement to lease capacity at Nscale's planned AI data centre in Essex, billed as the UK's largest, citing concerns about power supply. Nscale says it is still committed to building the site. The Register reports that grid connection delays could push the UK's AI ambitions into the 2030s. Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at a former coal plant in Indiana, producing nearly 1 gigawatt, though the plant is years from completion.

stories.headline: US orders federal agencies to remove DeepSeek, as DeepSeek reportedly helps Huawei design AI chips and Beijing weighs AI export controls

The US is shutting Chinese models out of government, while China is pairing its leading lab with a domestic chipmaker and considering restrictions on its own technology leaving the country. stories.headline: A hacker used a swarm of AI agents to breach more than 100 websites, as Microsoft starts treating agents as insider threats
stories.what_happened: The security firm Norforge says a hacker broke into more than 100 websites using AI agents that mostly operated on their own; Reuters reports the victims included John Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins. Microsoft released security tools in Microsoft 365 E7 and a system called Project Perception that continuously assess AI agents as potential insider threats. Ahold Delhaize confirmed that 'malicious actions' forced it to take systems offline across most of its US and European grocery brands. Separately, investigators pursuing ShinyHunters, which stole FBI data and is linked to a Florida DMV breach, have identified executives at two ransomware negotiation firms with unusually close ties to the group, according to Krebs on Security.
stories.why_it_matters: Autonomous agents make it far cheaper to attack many targets at once, and defenders are starting to treat their own agents as a risk inside the network. Repeated attacks on grocery chains show that ordinary consumers are directly affected.

A court filing says a member of the Saudi military paid for one-way tickets for his wife and son to return to Saudi Arabia. Prosecutors argue he should stay in detention because of 'considerable support from a foreign government'. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
stories.why_it_matters: If the allegations are proven, it would be a clear case of a state targeting a frontier AI lab, which supports the view that AI companies are now intelligence targets. That will add to pressure for stronger security at the labs.

stories.headline: US Supreme Court leaves intact a ruling that copyright termination can recover foreign rights, after four justices sit out
stories.what_happened: The US Supreme Court left intact a far-reaching Fifth Circuit ruling that US copyright termination can recover foreign rights granted in a worldwide deal. It did not reject the appeal by BMG, Sony Music, UMG and Warner Music on the merits: four justices sat out, so the court did not have enough members to hear it. The court also refused to hear Google's challenge to the USPTO using a patent's age ('settled expectations') as a reason to refuse review, and declined a copyright case over footage of Blackbeard's shipwreck.
stories.why_it_matters: Songwriters and other creators who use termination rights could recover worldwide rights, not only US rights, which affects the value of large music catalogues. Leaving the USPTO's 'settled expectations' practice in place makes it harder to challenge older patents at the PTAB.

whats_new.before: The Fifth Circuit ruling was under appeal, and the USPTO's discretionary denials were being challenged.
whats_new.now: Both stand for now, without a Supreme Court ruling on the merits.

stories.headline: European patent courts side with patent holders: a German injunction hits SAP Signavio and the UPC upholds Align's aligner patent
stories.what_happened: A German court granted an injunction against SAP's Signavio software after a challenge from Celonis. SAP says the ruling restricts only one specific process, not the whole product. The UPC's Paris local division upheld Align Technology's patent EP 2 237 738 on orthodontic appliances in its dispute with Angelalign. An EPO Board of Appeal decision on empagliflozin (T 0251/25) shows the limits of relying on clinical data published after the filing date.
stories.why_it_matters: Injunctions remain a strong tool in Europe, including against major software vendors, and they give patent holders leverage in licensing talks. The empagliflozin decision is a reminder for pharma applicants to include supporting data when they file.

whats_new.before: Recent European decisions had gone against several pharma originators, and the UK kept SEP injunctions.
whats_new.now: There is a software injunction in Germany and a UPC win for a medical device patent holder.

stories.headline: Renault joins Avanci's Wi-Fi 6 vehicle licence, as the pool says it has 'critical mass' for 5G in China
stories.what_happened: Renault is the latest licensee of Avanci's Wi-Fi 6 Vehicles programme, joining Mercedes-Benz, General Motors, Ford and Volvo Cars. Avanci's 5G head, Laurie Fitzgerald, told IAM that the pool has 'critical mass' in China, though negotiations continue, and that it wants to apply the same model to new adjacent markets. Separately, an IAM-reported study confirms that Rio de Janeiro's court grants more patent injunctions than São Paulo's, making forum choice within Brazil an important tactic.
stories.why_it_matters: Patent pools are becoming the standard way to license car connectivity, and they are expanding from cellular into Wi-Fi and other markets. Brazil is emerging as a jurisdiction where SEP holders can obtain injunctions.

signals.title: Cost-of-living anger is spreading across Europe and reaching bond markets
signals.what: In one weekend, protests over living costs turned violent in France and spread to Italy, Belgium and Albania, while housing protesters camped in Lisbon and Porto and Portugal's rent law began to lose its parliamentary support.
signals.why_it_matters: Energy costs from the Iran war, housing shortages and tight budgets are combining. Unrest is already lifting French borrowing costs and changing what governments can pass, from rent reform in Portugal to budgets in France.
signals.would_confirm: Protests continuing for weeks, more governments retreating on budget or housing reforms, and a further widening of southern European bond spreads.
signals.would_invalidate: Protests fading after the curfews and bond spreads narrowing again.

signals.title: Power, not chips, is becoming the limit on AI expansion
signals.what: Microsoft abandoned the UK's largest planned AI data centre over grid supply, while Amazon is paying for its own nuclear reactors. This follows warnings about data-centre power demand in Ireland.
signals.why_it_matters: Where electricity can be secured will shape where AI capacity, jobs and tax revenue end up. Combined with investors' doubts about AI returns, power delays could hold back the build-out.
signals.would_confirm: More hyperscaler withdrawals from projects with grid delays, and more own-generation deals.
signals.would_invalidate: Rapid grid-connection reforms in the UK and EU that restore cancelled projects.

signals.title: Tech supply chains are separating from both sides
signals.what: The US banned DeepSeek from federal systems and threatened Europe over satellite spectrum. China added export controls on construction machinery, is considering controls on AI models and chips, and is restricting foreign biotech deals.
signals.why_it_matters: Technology access is becoming a lever in relations between the US, China and Europe, so companies face rising compliance costs and less certain access to markets.
signals.would_confirm: Formal Chinese AI export rules, EU spectrum rules that exclude non-EU operators, or US trade action against Europe.
signals.would_invalidate: A US–China deal on technology trade, or the EU backing away from spectrum limits.

signals.title: AI companies are trying to win public trust
signals.what: Anthropic committed equity to a public fund and gave an outside watchdog independent access, Musk matched with a share pledge, and Democrats are preparing to scrutinise the industry, while a court filing alleges a state-linked effort to spy on OpenAI.
signals.why_it_matters: With public fears about AI rising before the midterms and before large IPOs, companies are offering visible commitments. Whether they hold up will affect future regulation.
signals.would_confirm: Other labs announcing similar funds or external oversight, or such commitments written into law.
signals.would_invalidate: The pledges stalling for lack of detail, or regulation going ahead regardless of them.
